facts.claim: OAIC, 'What is personal information?' (published 10 March 2023, modified 5 September 2024, read 23 November 2026): 'Personal information includes a broad range of information, or an opinion, that could identify an individual. What is personal information will vary, depending on whether a person can be identified or is reasonably identifiable in the circumstances.'

OAIC (same page): 'For example, personal information may include: an individual's name, signature, address, phone number or date of birth', and the list also includes 'sensitive information', 'photographs', 'internet protocol (IP) addresses' and 'location information from a mobile device'. (The page does not mention email addresses by name; do not say OAIC lists email.)

OAIC (same page, 'What is sensitive information?'): 'Sensitive information is personal information that includes information or an opinion about an individual's:' and the list includes 'health or genetic information'. The page does not mention dietary requirements or allergies; linking allergy questions to health information is the article's framing, not OAIC's words.
OAIC (same page): 'Generally, sensitive information has a higher level of privacy protection than other personal information.'

Reused from content/posts/wedding-photo-app/03-source-pack.json (fact_11). OAIC, 'Photos and videos' (page modified 26 September 2024): 'If the photo or video was taken by someone acting in a personal capacity, the Privacy Act doesn't apply — because it doesn't cover individuals.' (Context is photos; dash quoted as published, do not reuse in body copy. Apply to RSVP data only as 'the Privacy Act doesn't cover individuals acting in a personal capacity', as general information.)

Reused from content/posts/wedding-photo-app/03-source-pack.json (fact_12). OAIC (same page): 'In some situations, there may be state or territory laws that prevent someone photographing your private activities without your consent.' (Context is photography; for RSVPs say only that state or territory laws may also apply.)

Reused from content/posts/wedding-photo-app/03-source-pack.json (fact_14). OAIC (same page): 'The Privacy Act covers organisations with an annual turnover of more than $3 million that operate in Australia, and some other organisations.' (A legal threshold, not a price. Do not state whether any RSVP platform is covered.)

Australian Cyber Security Centre, cyber.gov.au, 'Learn about phishing scams' (no last-updated date shown, read 23 November 2026): 'Quishing is a type of phishing that uses QR codes instead of text-based links. QR codes are often trusted, but cybercriminals can use them to hide harmful links.'

cyber.gov.au (same page): 'Quishing is harder to detect than normal phishing because QR codes are images, not text. This means security tools may miss harmful links and you can’t check the link before scanning it.'

cyber.gov.au (same page, 'What you can do about phishing'): 'Be careful with messages and calls: don’t click links, scan QR codes or download files you weren’t expecting.' and 'Use trusted sources: go directly to official websites or use known phone numbers instead of links in messages.'
cyber.gov.au (same page, workplace practices): 'Use secure QR tools: create QR codes using trusted and secure tools.' (Written for workplaces; quote as general guidance only.)

insider_details.detail: An RSVP form collects names, addresses and phone numbers, which OAIC gives as examples of personal information, so ask only for what the planning actually needs and keep the guest list somewhere you trust. General information, not legal advice.

Dietary and allergy questions can touch on health details, and OAIC lists health information as sensitive information with generally higher protection. Ask for what the caterer needs ('any allergies we should share with the chef?') rather than medical detail, and share it only with suppliers who need it. General information, not legal advice.

OAIC says the Privacy Act doesn't cover individuals acting in a personal capacity, but state or territory laws may apply and the platform you choose may have its own obligations. Phrase as 'as at November 2026', general information only; the Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

On invitations and welcome signs, print the RSVP web address beside the QR code so guests can type it instead, since cyber.gov.au notes you can't check a QR link before scanning it and advises going directly to official websites.
Generate the QR code with a trusted tool and test-scan the printed proof before the print run; cyber.gov.au's workplace guidance is to 'create QR codes using trusted and secure tools'.
